video:video.video:title: How the Rolex Submariner Conquered the Deep
video:video.video:description: A dive watch has to do more than keep water out. It has to be readable when light and conditions change. This documentary follows the Rolex Submariner from the growth of scuba to its elapsed-time bezel, changing depth ratings and life beyond diving. It also separates the Submariner from the experimental Deep Sea Special carried outside Trieste and the Sea-Dweller's helium escape valve.

video:video.video:title: The Watch That Saved D-Day
video:video.video:description: Before the aircraft depart, four pathfinder officers synchronize their watches. That small ritual opens a different view of D-Day: weather, tides, airborne troops, naval support and beach demolition teams racing to connect a vast plan. Follow the operation from England to Normandy, including the changing tide and Omaha's obstacle-clearing deadline. The title describes the wristwatch's contribution to coordination; the historical photograph does not identify one miracle watch or a brand that decided the battle.

video:video.video:title: Why Paul Newman's Rolex Sold for $17.8 Million
video:video.video:description: A steel Rolex sold for $17.8 million in 2017. Follow Paul Newman's Daytona through Joanne Woodward's gift, racing, a treehouse and the evidence tying one watch to one life. We separate the dial nickname from ownership. Auction totals include buyer's premium; record claims refer to 2017.

video:video.video:title: Cartier Santos: The Flying Problem That Created a Luxury Icon
video:video.video:description: A luxury icon began with a flying problem. Before airline lounges and modern cockpits, Alberto Santos-Dumont was taking experimental machines over Paris. Cartier traces the Santos to a watch he could read without reaching into his pocket. This documentary follows the Eiffel Tower challenge, the 1904 origin story, the 14-bis, and the design that became recognizable far beyond aviation. Modern Santos watches illustrate the design story; they are not presented as the original watch flown by Santos-Dumont. Clearly labeled AI sequences are illustrative reconstructions or watch visualizations, not authentic historical footage.

video:video.video:title: The Watch That Helped Save Apollo 13 | Omega Speedmaster
video:video.video:description: A damaged spacecraft. A manual engine burn. One backup that could still count the seconds. The Omega Speedmaster played a small but practical role in Apollo 13's return. This documentary follows NASA's testing of the watch, its earlier place in Apollo 11, and the 14.8-second course correction that helped bring the crew home. The rescue belonged to Jim Lovell, Fred Haise, Jack Swigert, and the teams in Houston. How much did the watch really do?

video:video.video:title: The Watch That Refused to Break — How G-Shock Conquered the World
video:video.video:description: In 1984, a hockey player took a slapshot at a wristwatch on American television. The watch survived. Nobody believed it — until a news programme repeated the test live on air. This is the story of the G-Shock: the watch Kikuo Ibe built after his father's watch shattered on a Tokyo street, the two hundred prototypes he destroyed getting there, and the bouncing rubber ball that finally solved it.

video:video.video:title: How Rolex Became the Watch of Presidents
video:video.video:description: In December 1957 — three years before John F. Kennedy was even elected — a Rolex ad in an Italian newspaper already called the bracelet "President." Nobody in that ad was a president. The Day-Date arrived in 1956 as Rolex's flagship: gold or platinum only, with the day of the week spelled out in full. The word "President" was already in the catalogue before any president was known to wear one. Lyndon Johnson made it stick — but he didn't name it, and he didn't start a line of succession. The 1966 "presidents' watch" advertisement, the auction catalogues, the book titles and the newspaper shorthand did the rest. This is the story of a nickname that became the name — and of the myths that grew around it.

video:video.video:title: The Seiko That Changed Time Forever: How Quartz Started a Watch Revolution
video:video.video:description: On Christmas Day, 1969, Seiko released the Quartz Astron 35SQ: a gold watch almost nobody could afford. Inside was a technology that would make accurate time available to nearly everyone — and force Switzerland’s watch industry to find a new reason to matter. This is the story of the Seiko Astron, Project 59A, the Swiss Beta 21, and the quartz crisis that changed what a watch could mean.
